column1: Table 46.9  Recommended Treatment Approaches to Hypertensive Emergencies Acute Target-Organ Damage Timing for Acute BP Reductiona  Preferred Intravenous Drugsb    Diffuse microvascular injury ("malignant hypertension")c  Decrease BP by 20%-25% during first hour and to 160/100 mm Hg by 2-6 h  Labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside    Hypertensive encephalopathy  Decrease BP by 20%-25% during first hour and to 160/100 mm Hg by 2-6 h  Labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside; avoid hydralazine    Acute intracerebral hemorrhage  If systolic BP is 150-220 mm Hg, decrease systolic BP to 140-150 mm Hg within 1 h, particularly in patients without known hypertension and those with underlying vascular abnormalities, such as aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations. In patients with large hematoma volume and evidence of increased intracranial pressure, BP management should be more liberal (keep systolic BP <180 mm Hg). Lowering systolic BP below 140 mm Hg may be harmful.  Labetalol, nicardipine, devidipine, nitroprusside; avoid hydralazine    Acute ischemic stroke  If thrombolytic therapy is indicated, decrease BP to <185/110 mm Hg before giving thrombolytic agents and maintain BP <180/105 mm Hg for the first 24 h. If thrombolytic therapy is not indicated and there is no acute target-organ damage other than stroke, the strategy depends on BP. If BP is <220/120 mm Hg, no intervention is indicated for the first 48-72 h. If BP is 2220/120 mm Hg or there is other acute target-organ damage, such as heart failure or myocardial infarction, decrease BP by 15% within 1 h.  Labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside; avoid hydralazine    Acute coronary syndromes  Decrease systolic BP to <140 mm Hg within 1 h; keep diastolic BP >60 mm Hg  Nitroglycerin, labetalol, esmolol, metoprolol; avoid hydralazine    Acute heart failure  Decrease systolic BP to <140 mm Hg within 1 h  Nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, loop diuretics needed in most cases; enalaprilat or hydralazine may be useful; avoid β-blockers    Aortic dissection  Decrease both systolic BP to <120 mm Hg and heart rate to <60 beats/min within 20 min  Esmolol (or labetalol) plus one of nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside, or nitroglycerin; both a beta-blocker (unless bradycardia is already present) and a vasodilator should be used <sup>a</sup>Initiation, reinstatement, or adjustments of long-acting oral antihypertensive medications should take place during the first 6 to 12 hours. Oral drugs are chosen on the basis of conventional guidelines. Intravenous medications can be tapered on the basis of observed blood pressure levels after the addition of oral agents. <sup>b</sup>Nitroprusside continues to be a recommended agent by most guidelines. Given its potential toxicity, it should be avoided as a first choice when other options are available. <sup>c</sup>Diffuse microvascular injury is identified as high-grade retinopathy (hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema), acute kidney injury, or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia present alone or in combination. BP, Blood pressure.
